mosasaurus:enwiki:13.title: Mosasaurus (Phylogeny and evolution of the genus)

facts.statement: The first fossils of Mosasaurus were discovered as skulls in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in the late 18th century.
facts.quote: the first fossils of Mosasaurus were found as skulls in a chalk quarry near the Dutch city of Maastricht in the late 18th century

facts.statement: A skull discovered in 1778 was nicknamed the "great animal of Maastricht".
facts.quote: One skull discovered in 1778 was famously nicknamed the "great animal of Maastricht".

facts.statement: In 1808, Georges Cuvier concluded that Mosasaurus was a giant marine lizard similar to monitor lizards but unlike any living animal at the time.
facts.quote: In 1808, naturalist Georges Cuvier concluded that it belonged to a giant marine lizard with similarities to monitor lizards but otherwise unlike any known living animal.

facts.statement: William Daniel Conybeare named the genus Mosasaurus in 1822, referencing the Meuse River where the fossils were found.
facts.quote: William Daniel Conybeare in 1822 when he named it Mosasaurus in reference to its origin in fossil deposits near the Meuse River.

facts.statement: The first known Mosasaurus fossil, a skull discovered in 1764 near Maastricht, was initially misidentified as a whale.
facts.quote: The first Mosasaurus fossil known to science was discovered in 1764 in a chalk quarry near Maastricht in the Netherlands in the form of a skull, which was initially identified as a whale.

facts.statement: A second skull found in 1778 was initially thought to be a crocodile by Johann Leonard Hoffmann.
facts.quote: Later, in 1778, the quarry produced a second skull that caught the attention of Johann Leonard Hoffmann, who thought it was a crocodile.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell named the species Mosasaurus hoffmanni in 1829 to honor Johann Leonard Hoffmann.
facts.quote: In 1829, Gideon Mantell added the specific epithet hoffmanni, in honor to Hoffmann.

facts.statement: The largest species, Mosasaurus hoffmanni, could reach a maximum length of 12 meters.
facts.quote: The largest species, M. hoffmanni, is estimated to measure up to 12 m in maximum length.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had four limbs shaped into paddles used for steering underwater.
facts.quote: Its four limbs were shaped into paddles to steer the animal underwater.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence indicates Mosasaurus inhabited much of the Atlantic Ocean and adjacent seaways.
facts.quote: Fossil evidence suggests Mosasaurus inhabited much of the Atlantic Ocean and the adjacent seaways.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus fossils have been found in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and Antarctica.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus fossils have been found in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and Antarctica.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence documents an instance of the mosasaur Tylosaurus attacking a Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: There were still conflicts among them, as an instance of Tylosaurus attacking a Mosasaurus has been documented.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus likely fought using snout grappling, a behavior similar to that seen in modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Fighting likely took place in the form of snout grappling, as seen in modern crocodiles.

facts.statement: Scientists continue to debate whether the closest living relatives of Mosasaurus are monitor lizards or snakes.
facts.quote: The exact affinities of Mosasaurus as a squamate remain controversial, and scientists continue to debate whether its closest living relatives are monitor lizards or snakes.

facts.statement: More than fifty species were once attributed to the genus Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: As a result, more than fifty species have been attributed to the genus in the past.

facts.statement: A 2017 redescription of the type specimen confirmed at least four other species belong within the genus Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: A redescription of the type specimen in 2017 helped resolve the taxonomy issue and confirmed at least four other species to be within the genus.

facts.statement: A fossil skeleton identified as a 49-foot-long fish was discovered by the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1804 near the Missouri River.
facts.quote: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition discovered a now-lost fossil skeleton alongside the Missouri River, which was identified as a 49 ft long fish.

facts.statement: In 1818, a fossil from Monmouth County, New Jersey became the first North American specimen correctly identified as Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1818, a fossil from Monmouth County, New Jersey became the first North American specimen to be correctly recognized as a Mosasaurus by scientists of the time.

facts.statement: Richard Harlan first described the type specimen of M. missouriensis in 1834 using a snout fragment found near the Big Bend of a river in South Dakota.
facts.quote: The type specimen of M. missouriensis was first described in 1834 by Richard Harlan based on a snout fragment found near the river's Big Bend, in South Dakota.

facts.statement: Georg August Goldfuss published a study on the M. missouriensis fossil material in 1845.
facts.quote: Georg August Goldfuss in Bonn for research, who published a study in 1845.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy established the combination M. missouriensis in 1857 following a suggestion by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer.
facts.quote: Joseph Leidy erected the new combination M. missouriensis after this suggestion in 1857, which has since entered common use.

facts.statement: The missing snout fragment of the M. missouriensis type specimen was found in 2004 in the MNHN collections under catalog number MNHN 9587.
facts.quote: The snout was finally found in 2004 in the collections of the MNHN under the catalog number MNHN 9587, thus confirming the initial suspicion expressed by von Meyer and followed by other authors.

facts.statement: Louis Dollo first described M. lemonnieri in 1889 based on a specimen with a relatively complete skull and neck vertebrae found in a quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.
facts.quote: M. lemonnieri was first described in 1889 by Louis Dollo based on a specimen comprising a relatively complete skull and several cervical (neck) vertebrae, discovered in a quarry owned by the Solvay S.A. company in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.

facts.statement: The M. lemonnieri type specimen, numbered IRSNB R28, was donated by Alfred Lemonnier, after whom the species was named.
facts.quote: This specimen, since numbered as IRSNB R28, is one of the many fossils donated by the then director of the company, Alfred Lemonnier, Dollo naming the species in his honor.

facts.statement: Camille Arambourg named M. beaugei in 1952 as part of a research program on Moroccan phosphate deposits that began in 1934.
facts.quote: M. beaugei was named in 1952 by Camille Arambourg as part of a large-scale research program on the phosphate deposits of Morocco that had been ongoing since 1934.

facts.statement: M. beaugei was initially described from nine isolated teeth found in the Oulad Abdoun and Ganntour basins and dedicated to Alfred Beaugé, director-general of the OCP Group.
facts.quote: The species was initially described from nine isolated teeth discovered in the phosphate basins of Oulad Abdoun and Ganntour, and was dedicated to Alfred Beaugé, then director-general of the OCP Group, who supported Arambourg's research.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel demonstrated in 1854 that Mosasaurus possessed fully aquatic flippers rather than limbs for walking.
facts.quote: In 1854, Hermann Schlegel proved how Mosasaurus actually had fully aquatic flippers.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel showed that Mosasaurus phalanges lacked muscle or tendon attachments, proving that walking was impossible.
facts.quote: He clarified that earlier interpretations of claws were erroneous and demonstrated how the phalanges show no indication of muscle or tendon attachment, which would make walking impossible.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was a derived mosasaur characterized by advanced evolutionary traits including a fully aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus was a type of derived mosasaur, or a latecoming member with advanced evolutionary traits such as a fully aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had a streamlined body, an elongated tail with a downturned two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.
facts.quote: As such, it had a streamlined body, an elongated tail ending with a downturn supporting a two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.

facts.statement: Modern understanding indicates that derived mosasaurs like Mosasaurus were built similarly to ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales due to convergent evolution.
facts.quote: While in the past derived mosasaurs were depicted as akin to giant flippered sea snakes, it is now understood that they were more similar in build to other large marine vertebrates such as ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales through convergent evolution.

facts.statement: The taxonomic validity of M. lemonnieri has been the subject of long-standing debate.
facts.quote: The taxonomic validity of M. lemonnieri was long debated.

facts.statement: In 2004, Mulder, Cornelissen, and Verding suggested M. lemonnieri might be a juvenile form of M. hoffmanni, attributing differences to age-based variation.
facts.quote: In 2004, Eric Mulder, Dirk Cornelissen, and Louis Verding suggested M. lemonnieri could be a juvenile form of M. hoffmanni based on the argument that significant differences could be explained by age-based variation.

facts.statement: Subsequent research contested the juvenile hypothesis by highlighting major anatomical differences between M. lemonnieri and M. hoffmanni, especially in dentition.
facts.quote: However, this was contested by subsequent work that highlighted major anatomical distinctions between the two species, primarily in the dentition.

facts.statement: A 2026 revision by Sharpe and colleagues reaffirmed the validity of M. lemonnieri by identifying distinct autapomorphies, particularly in the cranium.
facts.quote: In a 2026 revision dedicated to the species, Henry S. Sharpe and colleagues reaffirmed the validity of the taxon by identifying several clear autapomorphies, particularly in the cranium.

facts.statement: Researchers once estimated that the jaw length of M. hoffmanni was one-tenth of its total body length.
facts.quote: the length of the jaw equalled one tenth of the body length in the species

facts.statement: Using a smaller partial jaw, another study estimated the maximum length of M. hoffmanni to be 17.6 meters.
facts.quote: estimated a larger maximum length of 17.6 m

facts.statement: The skull of Mosasaurus is conical and tapers to a short snout that extends slightly beyond the frontmost teeth.
facts.quote: The skull of Mosasaurus is conical and tapers off to a short snout which extends a little beyond the frontmost teeth

facts.statement: The snout of M. hoffmanni is blunt, whereas the snout of M. lemonnieri is pointed.
facts.quote: In M. hoffmanni, this snout is blunt, while in M. lemonnieri it is pointed

facts.statement: A single row of small pits called foramina lines the jawline above the gum line in Mosasaurus jaws.
facts.quote: a single row of small pits known as foramina are lined parallel to the jawline

facts.statement: In M. hoffmanni, the external nostril openings measure around 21% to 24% of the skull's length.
facts.quote: the external nares (nostril openings) are moderately sized and measure around 21–24% of the skull's length in M. hoffmanni

facts.statement: The eardrum in Mosasaurus resides within a round and concave depression on the outer surface of the quadrate bone called the tympanic ala.
facts.quote: the eardrum residing within a round and concave depression in the outer surface called the tympanic ala

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were specialized for cutting prey and featured highly prismatic surfaces with two opposite cutting edges.
facts.quote: The features of teeth in Mosasaurus vary across species, but unifying characteristics include a design specialized for cutting prey, highly prismatic surfaces (enamel circumference shaped by flat sides called prisms), and two opposite cutting edges.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were generally large and robust, except in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri which had more slender teeth.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus teeth are large and robust except for those in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri, which instead have more slender teeth.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of M. hoffmanni and M. missouriensis were finely serrated, whereas M. conodon and M. lemonnieri lacked serrations entirely.
facts.quote: The cutting edges in M. hoffmanni and M. missouriensis are finely serrated, while in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri serrations do not exist.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of M. beaugei were neither serrated nor smooth but possessed minute wrinkles called crenulations.
facts.quote: The cutting edges of M. beaugei are neither serrated nor smooth, but instead possess minute wrinkles known as crenulations.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus possessed four types of teeth classified by their location on the upper and lower jaw bones.
facts.quote: Like all mosasaurs, Mosasaurus had four types of teeth, classified based on the jaw bones they were located on.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were largely uniform in size and shape (homodont) except for the smaller pterygoid teeth.
facts.quote: The teeth were largely consistent in size and shape with only minor differences throughout the jaws (homodont) except for the smaller pterygoid teeth.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were thecodont, meaning their roots were deeply cemented within the jaw bone.
facts.quote: The dentition was thecodont (tooth roots deeply cemented within the jaw bone).

facts.statement: Mosasaurus constantly shed teeth through a process where a replacement tooth developed inside the root of the original tooth and pushed it out.
facts.quote: Teeth were constantly shed through a process where the replacement tooth developed within the root of the original tooth and then pushed it out of the jaw.

facts.statement: Chemical studies of a M. hoffmanni tooth showed odontoblasts deposited dentin at an average rate of 10.9 micrometers per day.
facts.quote: Chemical studies conducted on a M. hoffmanni maxillary tooth measured an average rate of deposition of odontoblasts, the cells responsible for the formation of dentin, at 10.9 um per day.

facts.statement: A nearly complete Mosasaurus skeleton (SDSM 452) possessed seven cervical vertebrae, thirty-eight dorsal vertebrae, eight pygal vertebrae, and sixty-eight caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: One of the most complete Mosasaurus skeletons in terms of vertebral representation (Mosasaurus sp.; SDSM 452) has seven cervical (neck) vertebrae, thirty-eight dorsal vertebrae (which includes thoracic and lumbar vertebrae) in the back, and eight pygal vertebrae (front tail vertebrae lacking haemal arches) followed by sixty-eight caudal vertebrae in the tail.

facts.statement: All Mosasaurus species had seven cervical vertebrae, while counts for other vertebrae varied among species.
facts.quote: All species of Mosasaurus have seven cervical vertebrae, but other vertebral counts vary among them.

facts.statement: Partial skeletons suggest M. conodon had up to thirty-six dorsal and nine pygal vertebrae, M. hoffmanni had up to thirty-two dorsal and ten pygal vertebrae, and M. missouriensis had around thirty-three dorsal, eleven pygal, and at least seventy-nine caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Various partial skeletons of M. conodon, M. hoffmanni, and M. missouriensis suggest M. conodon likely had up to thirty-six dorsal vertebrae and nine pygal vertebrae; M. hoffmanni had likely up to thirty-two dorsal vertebrae and ten pygal vertebrae; and M. missouriensis around thirty-three dorsal vertebrae, eleven pygal vertebrae, and at least seventy-nine caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had an unusually deep rib cage forming a semicircle, giving it a barrel-shaped chest compared to other mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Compared to other mosasaurs, the rib cage of Mosasaurus is unusually deep and forms an almost perfect semicircle, giving it a barrel-shaped chest.

facts.statement: Extensive cartilage likely connected the ribs to the sternum in Mosasaurus, facilitating breathing and compression in deep water.
facts.quote: Rather than being fused together, extensive cartilage likely connected the ribs with the sternum, which would have facilitated breathing movements and compression when in deeper waters.

facts.statement: The bone texture of Mosasaurus was virtually identical to modern whales, indicating high aquatic adaptation and neutral buoyancy.
facts.quote: The texture of the bones is virtually identical with in modern whales, which indicates Mosasaurus possessed a high range of aquatic adaptation and neutral buoyancy as seen in cetaceans.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had a tail structure similar to relatives like Prognathodon, which is known to have had a two-lobed tail.
facts.quote: The tail structure of Mosasaurus is similar to relatives like Prognathodon, in which soft tissue evidence for a two-lobed tail is known.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus forelimbs were wide and robust, with fan-shaped scapulae and humeri that were wider than tall.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Mosasaurus are wide and robust. The scapula and humerus are fan-shaped and wider than tall.

facts.statement: The ilium in Mosasaurus was rod-like and slender, being around 1.5 times longer than the femur in M. missouriensis.
facts.quote: The ilium is rod-like and slender; in M. missouriensis, it is around 1.5 times longer than the femur.

facts.statement: The Mosasaurus femur was about twice as long as it was wide, ending in articular facets meeting at an angle of approximately 120 degrees.
facts.quote: The femur itself is about twice as long as it is wide and ends at the distal side in a pair of distinct articular facets (of which one connects to the ilium and the other to the paddle bones) that meet at an angle of approximately 120°.

facts.statement: The compressed structure of the Mosasaurus forelimb paddle was well-suited for faster swimming.
facts.quote: The overall structure of the paddle is compressed, similar to in Plotosaurus, and was well-suited for faster swimming.

facts.statement: The Mosasaurus hindlimb paddle was supported by four sets of digits.
facts.quote: In the hindlimbs, the paddle is supported by four sets of digits.

facts.statement: Ambiguity in defining the genus Mosasaurus arose because 19th-century scientists did not provide a proper diagnosis during initial descriptions due to undefined nomenclatural rules.
facts.quote: Because nomenclatural rules were not well-defined at the time, 19th century scientists did not give Mosasaurus a proper diagnosis during its initial descriptions, which led to ambiguity in how the genus is defined.

facts.statement: Street's 2016 doctoral thesis proposed constraining Mosasaurus to four species (M. hoffmanni, M. missouriensis, M. lemonnieri, and a proposed M. glycys), viewing M. conodon and Pacific taxa as different genera and M. beaugei as a junior synonym of M. hoffmanni.
facts.quote: Street & Caldwell (2017) was derived from Street's 2016 doctoral thesis, which contained a phylogenetic study proposing the constraining of Mosasaurus into four speciesM. hoffmanni, M. missouriensis, M. lemonnieri, and a proposed new species M. glycyswith M. conodon and the Pacific taxa recovered as belonging to different genera and M. beaugei view as a junior synonym of M. hoffmanni.

facts.statement: In a 2026 revision, Sharpe and colleagues considered M. conodon a nomen dubium because its holotype was too fragmentary to be diagnostic.
facts.quote: In their 2026 revision of M. lemonnieri, Sharpe and colleagues consider M. conodon as a nomen dubium, deeming its holotype too fragmentary to be diagnostic.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus is the type genus of the family Mosasauridae and subfamily Mosasaurinae, and is a member of the order Squamata.
facts.quote: As the type genus of the family Mosasauridae and the subfamily Mosasaurinae, Mosasaurus is a member of the order Squamata (which comprises lizards and snakes).

facts.statement: Mosasaurus traditionally forms a tribe with genera Eremiasaurus, Plotosaurus, and Moanasaurus within the subfamily Mosasaurinae, variously called Mosasaurini or Plotosaurini.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus, along with mosasaur genera Eremiasaurus, Plotosaurus, and Moanasaurus traditionally form a tribe within the Mosasaurinae variously called Mosasaurini or Plotosaurini.

facts.statement: Russell published one of the earliest evolutionary studies of Mosasaurus in 1967.
facts.quote: One of the earliest relevant attempts at an evolutionary study of Mosasaurus was done by Russell in 1967.

facts.statement: Bell recognized Plotosaurus as a distinct genus in his 1997 study despite finding it closely related to Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: Bell (1997) nevertheless recognized Plotosaurus as a distinct genus.

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar studied the head musculature of Mosasaurus hoffmanni in 1995.
facts.quote: In 1995, Lingham-Soliar studied the head musculature of M. hoffmanni.

facts.statement: The rigid, shock-absorbent cranial structure of Mosasaurus likely enabled a powerful bite force.
facts.quote: This rigid but highly shock-absorbent structure of the cranium likely allowed a powerful bite force.

facts.statement: Massive magnus adductor muscles indicate that Mosasaurus hoffmanni was capable of enormous bite forces.
facts.quote: The magnus adductor muscles, which attach to the lower jaws to the cranium and have a major role in biting function, are massive, indicating M. hoffmanni was capable of enormous bite forces.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus used its tail for swimming.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus swam using its tail.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus used its elongated, paddle-like limbs as hydrofoils for maneuvering.
facts.quote: Its elongated paddle-like limbs functioned as hydrofoils for maneuvering the animal.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of a separated ilium in Mosasaurus hoffmanni suggests that powerful paddle movements sometimes caused bone damage from shearing forces.
facts.quote: The powerful forces resulting from use of the paddles may have sometimes resulted in bone damage, as evidenced by a M. hoffmanni ilium with significant separation of the bone's head from the rest of the bone likely caused by frequent shearing forces at the articulation joint.

facts.statement: Bone tissue structure suggests Mosasaurus had a metabolic rate higher than modern lizards and comparable to leatherback turtles, ichthyosaurs, and plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: The tissue structure of Mosasaurus bones suggests it had a metabolic rate much higher than modern squamates and its resting metabolic rate was between that of the leatherback sea turtle and that of ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was likely endothermic, maintaining a constant body temperature independent of the environment.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus was likely endothermic and maintained a constant body temperature independent of the external environment.

facts.statement: Endothermy is unique among lizards, with the Argentine black and white tegu being the only known exception capable of partial endothermy.
facts.quote: Such a trait is unique among squamates, the only known exception being the Argentine black and white tegu, which can maintain partial endothermy.

facts.statement: Endothermy may have allowed Mosasaurus to thrive in cold climates like Antarctica.
facts.quote: It may have also been a factor that allowed Mosasaurus to thrive in the colder climates of locations such as Antarctica.

facts.statement: Large scleral rings in Mosasaurus eye sockets suggest the animal had good vision.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus had relatively large eye sockets with large scleral rings occupying much of the sockets' diameter; the latter is correlated with eye size and suggests it had good vision.

facts.statement: Side-placed eye sockets in Mosasaurus provided a narrow 28.5° binocular field but excellent vision for processing the two-dimensional near-surface environment.
facts.quote: The eye sockets were located at the sides of the skull, which created a narrow field of binocular vision at around 28.5° but alternatively allowed excellent processing of a two-dimensional environment, such as the near-surface waters inhabited by Mosasaurus.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus lemonnieri had better-developed olfactory organs than Mosasaurus hoffmanni, though they remained small.
facts.quote: In M. lemonnieri, these olfactory organs, although still small, are better developed and have some components lacking in M. hoffmanni.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was likely not a scavenger because it had a poor sense of smell.
facts.quote: It is unlikely Mosasaurus was a scavenger as it had a poor sense of smell.

facts.statement: As one of the largest marine animals of its time, Mosasaurus possessed large, robust cutting teeth capable of handling virtually any animal.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus was among the largest marine animals of its time, and with its large, robust cutting teeth, scientists believe larger members of the genus would have been able to handle virtually any animal.

facts.statement: Recent 2024 research suggests that ambush predation may not have been the only hunting strategy for Mosasaurus hoffmanni.
facts.quote: Recent 2024 research, however, used a model to calculate M. hoffmannis acceleration capabilities. They concluded that ambush predation may not be the only hunting strategy for M. hoffmanni.

facts.statement: Chemical and structural data suggests that M. lemonnieri and M. conodon may have hunted in deeper waters.
facts.quote: Chemical and structural data in the fossils of M. lemonnieri and M. conodon suggests they may have also hunted in deeper waters.

facts.statement: Carbon isotope studies found extremely low δ13C values in M. hoffmanni fossils, the lowest recorded in all mosasaurs for the largest individuals.
facts.quote: Carbon isotope studies on fossils of multiple M. hoffmanni individuals have found extremely low values of δ13C, the lowest in all mosasaurs for the largest individuals.

facts.statement: Low δ13C levels in M. hoffmanni reinforce its likely position as an apex predator.
facts.quote: M. hoffmannis low δ13C levels reinforces its likely position as an apex predator.

facts.statement: Dental microwear indicates that M. hoffmanni had a generalist diet, a trait also seen in M. missouriensis.
facts.quote: Dental microwear has likewise shown that M. hoffmanni had a generalist diet, which also appears to be the case with M. missouriensis.

facts.statement: Only two Mosasaurus specimens with stomach contents are known, including a 75-million-year-old M. missouriensis containing dismembered remains of a 1-meter-long fish.
facts.quote: Currently, there are only two known examples of a Mosasaurus preserved with stomach contents. The first is a well-preserved partial skeleton of a small M. missouriensis dated about 75 million years old with dismembered and punctured remains of a 1 m long fish in its gut.

facts.statement: M. missouriensis consumed prey larger than its 66 cm skull by dismembering it and eating pieces at a time.
facts.quote: This fish was much longer than the length of the mosasaur's skull, which measured 66 cm in length, confirming that M. missouriensis consumed prey larger than its head by dismembering and consuming bits at a time.

facts.statement: Coexisting with Prognathodon, M. missouriensis likely specialized in prey best consumed with cutting teeth, demonstrating niche partitioning.
facts.quote: Due to coexistence with other large mosasaurs like Prognathodon, which specialized in robust prey, M. missouriensis likely specialized more on prey best consumed using cutting-adapted teeth in an example of niche partitioning.

facts.statement: A subadult M. hoffmanni skeleton nicknamed "Lars" was recovered near Maastricht and contains acid-corroded bones of a juvenile turtle and other unidentified animals in its gut region.
facts.quote: The second is from a subadult M. hoffmanni partial skeleton recovered from the same locality as the species' holotype near Maastricht, nicknamed "Lars".

facts.statement: An alternate explanation suggests the bite marks on a nautiloid were made by a single mosasaur biting with increasing force rather than by two different individuals.
facts.quote: An alternate explanation postulates the bite marks as from one individual mosasaur that lightly bit the nautiloid at first, then proceeded to bite again with greater force.

facts.statement: A partial M. conodon skeleton shows multiple cuts, breaks, punctures, and a tooth piercing the quadrate bone, indicating attacks from another M. conodon.
facts.quote: One partial skeleton of M. conodon bears multiple cuts, breaks, and punctures on various bones, particularly in the rear portions of the skull and neck, and a tooth from another M. conodon piercing through the quadrate bone.

facts.statement: The lack of healing on injuries in an M. conodon fossil suggests it was killed by a fatal blow to the skull during an attack.
facts.quote: No injuries on the fossil show signs of healing, suggesting that the mosasaur was killed by its attacker by a fatal blow in the skull.

facts.statement: Healing signs around a wound in an M. missouriensis skeleton imply that the individual survived an attack by another mosasaur.
facts.quote: In this case, there were signs of healing around the wound, implying survival of the incident.

facts.statement: Takuya Konishi suggested that an embedded tooth in an M. missouriensis skeleton might result from head-biting courtship behavior seen in modern lizards.
facts.quote: Takuya Konishi suggested an alternative cause of this example being head-biting behavior during courtship as seen in modern lizards.

facts.statement: Some M. hoffmanni jaws show evidence of infectious diseases caused by physical injuries.
facts.quote: There are some M. hoffmanni jaws with evidence of infectious diseases as a result of physical injuries.

facts.statement: Researchers speculated that an infected M. hoffmanni switched to a diet of soft-bodied prey like squid to minimize jaw use.
facts.quote: Schulp and colleagues speculated it switched to a foraging-type diet of soft-bodied prey like squid that could be swallowed whole to minimize jaw use.

facts.statement: Avascular necrosis has been reported in every examined specimen of M. lemonnieri and M. conodon.
facts.quote: Avascular necrosis has been reported by many studies to be present in every examined specimen of M. lemonnieri and M. conodon.

facts.statement: In 2005, Rothschild and Martin observed that avascular necrosis affected between 3-17% of the vertebrae in the spines of examined mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Rothschild and Martin in 2005 observed that the condition affected between 3-17% of the vertebrae in the mosasaurs' spines.

facts.statement: The presence of avascular necrosis indicates that both Mosasaurus species may have been habitual or repetitive deep-divers.
facts.quote: This indicates that both Mosasaurus species may have either been habitual deep-divers or repetitive divers.

facts.statement: Agnete Weinreich Carlsen suggested that avascular necrosis in Mosasaurus was a product of inadequate anatomical adaptation.
facts.quote: Agnete Weinreich Carlsen considered it the simplest explanation that such conditions were a product of inadequate anatomical adaptation.

facts.statement: Unnatural fusion of tail vertebrae occurs in Mosasaurus when bones remodel after damage from trauma or disease.
facts.quote: Unnatural fusion of tail vertebrae has been documented in Mosasaurus, which occurs when the bones remodel themselves after damage from trauma or disease.

facts.statement: A 2015 study found fused tail vertebrae in three of 15 surveyed Mosasaurus specimens from North America and Belgium.
facts.quote: A 2015 study by Rothschild and Everhart surveyed 15 Mosasaurus specimens from North America and Belgium and found cases of fused tail vertebrae in three of them.

facts.statement: Microanatomical studies show that juvenile Mosasaurus bone structures are comparable to those of adults.
facts.quote: Microanatomical studies on bones of juvenile Mosasaurus and related genera have found that their bone structures are comparable to adults.

facts.statement: Shallow ocean deposits containing juvenile Mosasaurus suggest that juveniles may have lived in shallow waters.
facts.quote: These localities are all shallow ocean deposits, suggesting that juvenile Mosasaurus may still have lived in shallow waters.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus fossils have been found in the Midwest and East Coast of the US, Canada, Europe, Turkey, Russia, the Levant, the African coastline from Morocco to South Africa, Brazil, Argentina, and Antarctica.
facts.quote: These localities include the Midwest and East Coast of the United States, Canada, Europe, Turkey, Russia, the Levant, the African coastline from Morocco to South Africa, Brazil, Argentina, and Antarctica.

facts.statement: During the Late Cretaceous, Mosasaurus inhabited the Atlantic Ocean, the Western Interior Seaway, and the Mediterranean Tethys.
facts.quote: During the Late Cretaceous, these regions made up the three seaways inhabited by Mosasaurus: the Atlantic Ocean, the Western Interior Seaway, and the Mediterranean Tethys.

facts.statement: The seaways inhabited by Mosasaurus encompassed tropical, subtropical, temperate, and subpolar climates.
facts.quote: Multiple oceanic climate zones encompassed the seaways, including tropical, subtropical, temperate, and subpolar climates.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus lived in the Mediterranean Tethys region, which covered modern-day Europe, Africa, and the Middle East during the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: The Mediterranean Tethys during the Maastrichtian stage was located in what is now Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest Mosasaurus also inhabited Atlantic regions including Brazil and New Jersey.
facts.quote: In recent studies, the confirmation of paleogeographical affinities extended this range to areas across the Atlantic including Brazil and the East Coast state of New Jersey.

facts.statement: The northern Tethyan margin, a habitat for Mosasaurus, was situated between 30°N and 40°N latitude, covering modern Europe, Turkey, and New Jersey.
facts.quote: The northern Tethyan margin was located around the paleolatitudes of 30–40°N, consisting of what is now the European continent, Turkey, and New Jersey.

facts.statement: The northern Tethyan margin featured a warm-temperate climate dominated by mosasaurs and sea turtles.
facts.quote: The margin provided a warm-temperate climate with habitats dominated by mosasaurs and sea turtles.

facts.statement: In areas like Belgium, Mosasaurus lemonnieri was the dominant species, found in greater numbers than other large mosasaurs.
facts.quote: In certain areas such as Belgium, other Mosasaurus species like M. lemonnieri were instead the dominant species, where its occurrences greatly outnumber those of other large mosasaurs.

facts.statement: The southern Tethyan margin, a habitat for Mosasaurus, lay between 20°N and 20°S, experiencing warm tropical climates.
facts.quote: The southern Tethyan margin was located along the equator between 20°N and 20°S, resulting in warmer tropical climates.

facts.statement: The southern Tethyan margin included vast shallow marine environments along the seabeds of Africa, Arabia, the Levant, and Brazil.
facts.quote: Seabeds bordering the cratons in Africa and Arabia and extending to the Levant and Brazil provided vast shallow marine environments.

facts.statement: The Western Interior Seaway where early Mosasaurus fossils were found was shallow, with a maximum depth of about 800 to 900 meters.
facts.quote: The region was shallow for a seaway, reaching a maximum depth of about 800-900 m.

facts.statement: The Western Interior Seaway had two subprovinces: a cool temperate northern region and a warm temperate to subtropical southern region.
facts.quote: The oceanic climate of the Northern Interior Subprovince was likely a cool temperate one, while the Southern Interior Subprovince had warm temperate to subtropical climates.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus remained the dominant genus in the Western Interior Seaway until the end of the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus continued to be the dominant genus in the seaway until the end of the Navesinkan Age at the end of the Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus fossils are known from late Maastrichtian deposits in the Antarctic Peninsula, specifically the López de Bertodano Formation on Seymour Island.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus is known from late Maastrichtian deposits in the Antarctic Peninsula, specifically the López de Bertodano Formation in Seymour Island.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus lived in Antarctic waters around 65°S where deep water averaged 6°C, surface waters could freeze, and sea ice may have formed.
facts.quote: Located within the polar circle at around 65°S, temperatures at medium to large water depths would have been around 6 C on average, while sea surface temperatures may have dropped below freezing and sea ice may have formed at times.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was the most diverse mosasaur group found in Maastrichtian Antarctica.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus appears to be the most diverse mosasaur in the Maastrichtian Antarctica.

facts.statement: It is debated whether some Antarctic Mosasaurus specimens actually belong to the genus Moanasaurus, pending a revision of that genus.
facts.quote: However, it is possible that such specimens may actually represent Moanasaurus, although this depends on the outcome of a pending revision of the genus.

facts.statement: The validity of some Antarctic mosasaur genera is disputed because they are based primarily on isolated teeth.
facts.quote: The validity of some of these genera is disputed as they are primarily based on isolated teeth.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus and Prognathodon were the dominant and ecologically diversified mosasaur taxa throughout the Mediterranean Tethys seaway.
facts.quote: The two mosasaurs Mosasaurus and Prognathodon appear to have been the dominant taxa, being widespread and ecologically diversified throughout the seaway.

facts.statement: The appearance of Mosasaurus species at 79.5 Ma caused a complete faunal turnover in the Western Interior Seaway, profoundly restructuring marine ecosystems.
facts.quote: The fossil assemblages throughout these regions suggest a complete faunal turnover when M. missouriensis and M. conodon appeared at 79.5 Ma, indicating that the presence of Mosasaurus in the Western Interior Seaway had a profound impact on the restructuring of marine ecosystems.

facts.statement: In the Southern Interior Subprovince, key genera including sharks and other mosasaurs disappeared and were replaced by Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: In what is now Alabama within the Southern Interior Subprovince, most of the key genera including sharks like Cretoxyrhina and the mosasaurs Clidastes, Tylosaurus, Globidens, Halisaurus, and Platecarpus disappeared and were replaced by Mosasaurus.

facts.statement: Marine ecosystems in the Western Interior Seaway were more diverse during the Niobraran Age before Mosasaurus appeared than during the subsequent Navesinkan Age.
facts.quote: The faunal structure of both provinces was generally much more diverse prior to the appearance of Mosasaurus, during a faunal stage known as the Niobraran Age, than it was during the following Navesinkan Age.

facts.statement: The genus Mosasaurus was named by Conybeare in 1822.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Conybeare, 1822

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Mosasaurus is Mosasaurus hoffmannii.
facts.quote: type_species: Mosasaurus hoffmannii

facts.statement: Mosasaurus lived between 70 and 66 million years ago in what are now Western Europe, North America, South America, and Antarctica.
facts.quote: hace entre 70-66 millones de años en el área de las actuales Europa Occidental, Norteamérica, Sudamérica y Antártida

facts.statement: The name Mosasaurus refers to the fact that the first specimen was found near the Meuse River.
facts.quote: Su nombre hace referencia al hecho de que el primer espécimen fue hallado cerca del río Mosa

facts.statement: The largest known species, Mosasaurus hoffmannii, could reach 18 meters in length.
facts.quote: La mayor especie conocida de este género es el Mosasaurus hoffmanni, el cual podía alcanzar los 18 metros de longitud

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was much more robust than tilosaurine mosasaurs of similar length.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus era mucho más robusto que los mosasaurios tilosaurinos de longitud similar

facts.statement: The skull was more strongly built than in other mosasaurs because the jaw articulated very tightly against the skull.
facts.quote: El cráneo estaba más fuertemente constituido que en otros mosasaurios, ya que la mandíbula se articulaba muy apretadamente contra el cráneo

facts.statement: Experts believe Mosasaurus lived near the ocean surface, feeding on fish, turtles, ammonites, and possibly smaller mosasaurs.
facts.quote: los expertos creen que Mosasaurus vivía cerca de la superficie del océano, donde se alimentaba de peces, tortugas, amonitas, y posiblemente mosasaurios más pequeños

facts.statement: The animal stayed near the surface and, although capable of diving, evidently preferred not to venture into deeper waters.
facts.quote: El animal permanecía cerca de la superficie y aunque era capaz de bucear, evidentemente prefería no aventurarse en aguas más profundas

facts.statement: Its paddle-shaped limbs had five digits on the front flippers and four on the rear flippers.
facts.quote: Sus miembros en forma de aletas contaban con cinco dígitos en las frontales y cuatro en las posteriores

facts.statement: The trunk ended in a strong tail with a fin at the tip, which was the animal's main means of locomotion in water rather than its flippers.
facts.quote: El tronco acababa en una fuerte cola dotada de aleta en su extremo, siendo el principal medio de locomoción del animal en el agua, más que sus aletas

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was the first mosasaur genus to be named (and in fact, the first prehistoric reptile genus to be named).
facts.quote: Mosasaurus fue el primer género de mosasaurio en ser nombrado (y de hecho, el primer género de reptil prehistórico que lo fue)

facts.statement: The first known scientific remains were skull fragments from a limestone quarry on Monte San Pedro, a hill near Maastricht, Netherlands, found in 1764.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos conocidos por la ciencia fueron unos fragmentos de cráneo provenientes de una cantera de calizas en el Monte San Pedro, una colina cerca de Maastricht, Países Bajos, hallados en 1764

facts.statement: The discovery was acquired by the Teylers Museum in Haarlem in 1784 by its first director, Martinus van Marum, who did not publish his description until 1790.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento fue adquirido por el Museo Teylers en Haarlem en 1784 por Martinus van Marum, el primer director del museo, quien no publicó su descripción hasta 1790

facts.statement: Van Marum considered it to be a species of "great breathing fish" (Pisces cetacei), in other words, a whale.
facts.quote: Consideró que se trataba de una especie de "gran pez que respira" (Pisces cetacei, en otras palabras: una ballena)

facts.statement: A retired Dutch/German army physicist, Johann Leonard Hoffmann, also found some fragments and wrote a letter to the Dutch professor Petrus Camper about the skull.
facts.quote: Un físico retirado del ejército holandés/alemán, Johann Leonard Hoffmann (1710-1782), también encontró algunos fragmentos y escribió por carta sobre el cráneo al profesor neerlandés Petrus Camper

facts.statement: Hoffmann presumed the animal was a crocodile.
facts.quote: Hoffmann presumía que el animal era un cocodrilo

facts.statement: However, in 1786 Camper disagreed and concluded the remains were from "an unknown toothed whale."
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en 1786 Camper no estuvo de acuerdo y concluyó que los restos eran de "una ballena dentada desconocida"

facts.statement: In 1798, Petrus Camper's son, Adriaan Gilles Camper, studied the fossil again indirectly by reconsidering the description made by his father.
facts.quote: En 1798 el hijo de Petrus Camper, Adriaan Gilles Camper, estudió de nuevo al fósil indirectamente al reconsiderar la descripción hecha por su padre

facts.statement: He was the first to conclude that the remains belonged to a giant monitor lizard.
facts.quote: Él fue el primero en llegar a la conclusión de que los restos pertenecían a un lagarto varano gigante

facts.statement: However, as Dutch historian Peggy Rompen has shown, very little of this famous story can be corroborated by other sources.
facts.quote: No obstante, como ha mostrado la historiadora neerlandesa Peggy Rompen, muy poco de esta famosa historia puede ser corroborado por otras fuentes

facts.statement: William Daniel Conybeare named the genus Mosasaurus in 1822 after the Maas (Meuse) river, designating the second skull found as the holotype.
facts.quote: En 1822 William Daniel Conybeare lo nombró Mosasaurus por el nombre latino (Mosa) del río Maas (o Meuse) que pasa junto al monte Saint Peter, siendo el segundo cráneo el holotipo, MNHNP AC9648.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell added the species name hoffmannii in 1829 to honor Hoffmann, assuming he was the discoverer of the type specimen.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie (epíteto) hoffmannii fue añadido por Gideon Mantell en 1829, en homenaje a Hoffmann, bajo la suposición de que era el descubridor del espécimen tipo.

facts.statement: German biologist Hermann Schlegel was the first to conjecture in 1854 that Mosasaurus possessed flippers instead of clawed legs.
facts.quote: En 1854 el biólogo alemán Hermann Schlegel fue el primero en conjeturar que Mosasaurus tenía aletas en vez de patas con garras.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus belongs to the subfamily Mosasaurinae within the family Mosasauridae.
facts.quote: La familia Mosasauridae se divide en varias subfamilias, siendo Mosasaurus situado en Mosasaurinae.

facts.statement: Within the subfamily Mosasaurinae, Mosasaurus is associated with Clidastes, Moanasaurus, Amphekepubis, and Liodon in the tribe Mosasaurini.
facts.quote: Esta subfamilia, a su vez, se divide en agrupaciones menores o tribus, en las que Mosasaurus se asocia con Clidastes, Moanasaurus, Amphekepubis y Liodon en la tribu Mosasaurini.
